passages.t: Cast your bread upon the waters
passages.happening:
“Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again” (verse 1). ‘Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what disaster may befall the land’ (verse 2).

When clouds are full they pour out rain, and where a tree falls, there it lies (verse 3). ‘He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap’ (verse 4).

‘As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things’ (verse 5). So ‘Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 closed a long collection on wisdom and folly. Chapter 11 turns to urging, and the tone becomes more urgent and more hopeful. The Teacher has shown again and again that people cannot know the future. Here he draws the practical conclusion: not knowing is not a reason to freeze. It is a reason to act, to give and to enjoy.

Verse 1 has been read in two main ways. The older reading, in Jewish and Christian tradition alike, hears a call to generosity: give freely, even when it seems wasted, and it will come back. Many modern commentators hear a picture of trade by sea: send your grain across the water, and after many days you will see a return. Israel traded by sea mostly through Phoenician partners, and Solomon's ships are said to have come back once every three years. Verse 2 fits either reading, as generosity to many people or as spreading risk across several ventures. Seven, even eight, is a Hebrew way of saying many.

Farmers watched the wind and clouds anxiously at sowing and harvest. The one who waits for perfect weather never plants.

The word in verse 5 can mean wind or spirit, so the verse may speak of how the wind blows, or of how the breath of life enters a child in the womb. Either way, some of God's work is beyond human sight.
passages.later: The psalm says what verse 5 says about the womb: ‘My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret’ (Psalm 139:15). And Paul uses the picture of sowing: ‘whoever sows generously will also reap generously’ (2 Corinthians 9:6).
passages.asks: The one who waits for perfect conditions never sows. Ask what good thing you are putting off until you are sure of the outcome. And ask where you could give generously this week without knowing how it will return.

passages.t: Light is sweet: rejoice in your youth
passages.happening:
‘Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun’ (verse 7). ‘So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many’ (verse 8).

“Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment” (verse 9).

‘So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are fleeting’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Light and darkness frame verses 7 and 8. Life under the sun is sweet, and it is also short, with dark days ahead.

Verse 10 ends with hevel, translated fleeting. Here the word plainly means brief, like breath. Youth does not last.

The chapter break is a little artificial. The thought runs straight on into 12:1: remember your Creator in the days of your youth. Chapters 11 and 12 together are the book's closing appeal before the narrator's last words.
passages.later: The law warned Israel about the heart and eyes of verse 9: that they should remember the LORD's commandments and not go after ‘your own heart and your own eyes’ (Numbers 15:39). And the next verse of Ecclesiastes carries the call on: ‘Remember your Creator in the days of your youth’ (Ecclesiastes 12:1).
passages.hard:
Is the Teacher telling young people to follow whatever their heart desires?

Verse 9 says to walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, which sounds like permission for anything. Some readers notice that Numbers 15:39 warns Israel not to follow their own heart and eyes, and they see a tension.

But the Teacher adds at once: know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment. His point is not that desire is a reliable guide. It is that the young should take hold of life with energy and delight, knowing that they answer to God for how they do it.

The judgment clause is not a threat that cancels the joy. It is the frame that makes joy responsible. The next verse's call to banish sorrow shows that the Teacher means wholehearted, grateful living, not reckless indulgence. Life is a gift to enjoy and a trust to answer for, and the chapter holds both together, as the rest of Scripture does.
passages.asks: Light is sweet, and youth is fleeting. If you are young, ask what joy God is giving you now that you have been too busy or too anxious to receive. And whatever your age, ask how you might live gladly today, knowing you will give an account of it to God.
